utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor verse Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 24th of March, 2009. I would like to welcome the accused, the Defence counsel, the witness, as well as the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom much. Registrar, have you two IC numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It is actually three. The 2D Defence has submitted its objections to documents tendered by the Prosecution, and the Petkovic Defence team, through witness Bandic, Ivan. The Prosecution has also submitted its combined objections to Defence list of documents through witness Bandic, Ivan. This list shall be given Exhibit numbers IC961, 962 and 963 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Registrar. Ms. Nozica, I believe have you 18 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, and good afternoon, Mr. Makar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Makar, at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, we spoke about your contacts between Mr. Saric, the commander of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army and Dr. Ivo Prodan, head of department, who was employed in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, in the Health Administration. Can you tell me, to the best of your knowledge, and looking at the Medical Corps and field of Health, was there any cooperation between the Republic of Croatia and the 2nd Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I can confirm that. Mr. Prodan and the Administration for Health of Croatia helped us a great deal in supplying the 2nd Corps with sanitary material, medicines, and in setting up wartime hospitals, and in equipping those hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like us now to look at a few documents and to have your comments. The first is 2D1132. And I hope you have the binder.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't seem to have the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could I ask the usher to help us out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll take them in order, so find 2D1132 first, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain what this document represents? What is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document. It's a command, ordering Dr. Ivan Hudolin to take up the position of the coordinator for civilian and military health in the territory of the Operative Group East Posavina, and he is appointed as the chief surgeon at the war hospital at Brcko. I knew Mr. Hudolin, I knew him then and I know him now, and I know that he did take up that post. I visited the war hospital frequently so I can confirm that that's what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at the next document, 2D1133.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, once again this is a document that refers to Dr. Hudolin, regulating some of his rights in the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at 2D1131, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another document connected to Dr. Hudolin's involvement, and by this order priority is given in traffic for him to be able to go about his duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is 2D1136. Would you take a look at that now, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document of the District Staff of the Territorial Defence, dated September 1992, signed by the corps commander, Zeljko Knez, and it is ordered hereby that the Administration for Health be established in the 2nd Corps, with its seat in Tuzla, and the commander is Dr. Mejrudin Hosonovic, and the deputy commander and chief inspector of the war hospitals is Dr. Ivan Hudolin. He was appointed to that post. So this confirms that pursuant to an order from Mr. Prodan and the minister of defence, Dr. Hudolin came to the corps, was engaged by the corps to carry out these duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is 2D1137, once against signed by Zeljko Knez.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document follows on from the other one, judging by the date, and the Command Staff of the war hospitals is determined, and locations for the formation of war hospitals are mentioned, and for the commander of the war hospitals we see, among other things, in Maoca, a place called Maoca, that Dr. Hudolin -- Ivan Hudolin is being appointed to that post. And the corps commander has signed it, Zeljko Knez.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where Maoca is, what country that's in, what state?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maoca is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is Bosanska Posavina, near Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just two more documents. 2D1134 is the next one. This is a document dated the 2nd of November, 1992. 2D1134 is the number.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document by the head of the Sanitary Inspection Service from the Republic of Croatia, Professor Josip Stojakovic, giving certain instructions. I assume this is to Dr. Ivan Hudolin, because it says to Dr. Ivan Hudolin, and then it says "Dear Ivo." So some guide-lines for Dr. Hudolin.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The KBC of Tuzla is mentioned there, Tuzla KBC, and this incorporates the situation in the Tuzla hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the clinical hospital centre of Tuzla is a large medical institution, it was during the war and still is, and the staff from the hospital was used for the war hospitals as well, and Dr. Hudolin played his part there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at the next document, 2D1135. This is the Command of the 108th Brigade, Brcko, the 10th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander who signed this document is Ramiz Pljakic of the 108th Brigade of the HVO at Posavina; and I can't remember exactly, but I see from the contents of this document that Dr. Hudolin was supposed to be moved to the war hospital in Tolisa. However, the commander of the 108th Brigade is requesting that Dr. Hudolin stay where he is because his services are needed. And I know that there was very heavy fighting at that time in 1992 with a lot of wounded, and I know that Dr. Hudolin, as a surgeon, saved many lives, and many others the life of Dr. Miludin Hosonovic mentioned a moment ago, who was seriously wounded. Yes, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said Miludin Hosonovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For those reason the request by the brigade commander to have Dr. Hudolin remain where he was and carry out his duties there is what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at 2D1188 [as interpreted], the last document in this series relating to this area. It is signed by Mr. Bagaric on the 3rd of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see from the document that it is about the Bosanska Bjela war hospital, and I should like to point out that we're dealing with November 1993 here, where the assistant to the minister of defence of the Healthcare Administration from Herceg-Bosna from Mostar is ordering that a war hospital at Bosanska Bjela be established and that Dr. Ivan Hudolin should be the head of that hospital, the commander of it, and that the war hospital should see to all the wounded and sick from the area of the Municipal Assembly of Brcko and the area of responsibility of the 108th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this hospital, did it also treat all the members of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that for certain because I was there. At the time in the zone of defence of the 108th HVO Brigade, we would have many people from other parts of the brigades coming in of the BH Army, the 2nd Corps, to reinforce the troops in battle, so that upon their arrival in the area of responsibility of the 108th Brigade, as it says in this document, they were taken care of medically and relied on this particular war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Makar, do you know whether the members of the 2nd Army were treated in -- 2nd Corps were treated in Croatia, if they are more serious cases, and particularly at the time when the war hospitals hadn't gotten going properly yet?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, that that did happen, and I know of specific cases they were treated in Split, wounded were treated in Split, and I think in other countries as well, but I know for sure that they were treated in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Makar, I'd just briefly like to go through some documents which, in fact, speak of these relationships -- the good relationships between the Command of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army and the HVO of the brigades to which -- which belonged to the 2nd Corps. So I'm going to show you four documents one by one now, and the first of these is 2D1123, and I'll have -- I'll invite your comments at the end of them. 2D1127 is the next one, 2D1128, and the fourth 2D1129. Mr. Makar, based on these documents, which are, in fact, messages of congratulation, can you tell us what the relations were between the Command of the 2nd Corps, of which you were a part, and the HVO brigades? And here we see the date is 1993, but I'm asking you about the entire period.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to the best of my knowledge there were many more documents of a similar nature. These are various messages of congratulation. I see here that someone has been promoted to a higher rank, so Juric, Zvonko, the commander of the 115th Brigade; Pejo Banovic, the president of the Tuzla HVO; these were all men who are in constant contact of the corps, and the corps commander was often invited to various celebrations, religious feast days and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wish to make a correction. On page 5, in line 18, instead of "2D1188," it should say "2D1138." And, finally - my time is running out - could you describe to Their Honours what your contacts with Bruno Stojic were like? You said there were several such contacts. Could you describe them for us, and could you explain how significant they were for the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I met Mr. Bruno Stojic for the first time when I first visited Mostar, and we saw yesterday that it was on the 23rd of February, 1992. After this, we met on two other occasions, in the course of my visits, and I can say that as regards the significance of the logistical assistance we received from the HVO and Mr. Stojic, in my estimation his attitude toward the 2nd Corps and our mutual struggle was exceptionally correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Makar, in these conversations when you were putting forward the viewpoints of the 2nd Corps, did Mr. Stojic support the joint struggle and the joint command in the 2nd Corps, and did Mr. Stojic or anyone else that you talked to in Mostar feel that this was not the right way to go about things?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had those meetings, both formal meetings and informal chats afterwards, and always the view was expressed that it was significant for Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the 2nd Corps to successfully defend the territory of the population there. Mr. Stojic knew well that in the 2nd Corps, brigades of the HVO and brigades of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were fighting together under a joint command. He knew also that in the brigades of the HVO and the brigades of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ethnic make-up was mixed. On one occasion, he even pointed out that it would be disastrous if the Croats were to retreat from those areas or flee or leave, because the Muslims would not be able to defend themselves alone. That's the extent to which the struggle there was a common one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Makar. Your Honours, I have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have two short questions for you, which are follow-up questions, which I believe are important. According to all the documents we have seen, which have been shown to you by Ms. Nozica, we have documents that establish, and this is undisputed, that in certain logistics centres, either in Zagreb or Grude, that the ABiH were procured in arms weapons for at least the entire beginning of 1993, as far as the last document is concerned the one we have in our binder is dated the 2nd of May, 1993; where it is stated that MTS is supplied. As far as you know, after the months of May, let's say June, July, August, September, November and December, was the arms supply continued or not, either supplies coming in from the Republic of Croatia or from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can confirm that this method of supply continued until the end of the war. It was more difficult in those areas where there were conflicts and problems, but throughout the war this was our method of supply. Without it, we would certainly not have been able to defend ourselves and preserve the territory and the people we were defending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question: I would like you to look at the last document, please. It will be easier for everyone. 2D1129. It's the last document in your binder. There we have it. So I must say that when I saw this document in B/C/S, it is a document which I find poses a number of problems. Do you realise, like I do, that this document is headed "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, I can absolutely confirm this, because I know Mr. Pejo Banovic very well. We often run into each other in Tuzla. This is certainly a document issued by the Croatian Community of Soli. Mr. Pejo Banovic frequently visited the corps commander both ex officio and because he wished to assist wherever he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have seen other documents. Just turn to document 1138, which is the document just before this one, document 1138.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1128? I can't see 38. Oh, excuse me, yes, yes, 38 is in front of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1138, look at the heading. Look at the heading of this document. It doesn't say "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," but it does say "Bosnia and Herzegovina," and just below that it says "Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna." As far as you are concerned, do you have an explanation to give us for the different headings we see in both these documents? One is dated the 3rd of November, 1993, and the last document is dated the 16th of December, 1993. Let's say that there is a month in between these two documents. Why is there this difference, this distinction? Maybe you have no explanation to give us, but if you do, I would find this extremely interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, looking at this, I do observe the difference, but I'm unable to explain the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Look at the coat of arms that is on the document, and then look at the coat of arms which is on the document 1129, which is the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What difference is there, as far as you're concerned? I can see what the difference is, but I had rather you tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document 1129 is a document issued by the Croatian Community of Soli, so this is probably their way of marking the memorandum. The previous document, 1138, is issued by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And you can't really see the complete symbol here, but it was the symbol of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you know how the HVO used to work in Tuzla, according to you, the Tuzla HVO was of the same kind as the one you would find in Capljina or in Mostar, or did you have the feeling that it was different, as we can see from the stamps, the headings, the titles of the documents, or the reference to the Croatian Community of Soli? Were there some differences, and if so, what were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, I cannot say anything about the difference you're asking about, because I think this would be a political assessment which I am unable to provide. As the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Corps, what mattered to me was that the brigades of the Croatian Defence Council carried out their combat assignments. At that time, I was not interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Your answer will be on the transcript, and I will perhaps ask the question of other witnesses who will appear in this court of law. I now turn to the other Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. The Defence of Mr. Coric has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good to everyone in and around the courtroom. We have no questions for the gentleman, although we do thank him for coming here to give his evidence, and we wish him safe passage back to his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to ask only one question of the witness. I have a document which I think is similar to the ones we have seen, so I would like to have the witness see it. Could the usher help us, please. [In English] The number of the document I will use is 3D00312.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I appear on behalf of General Praljak. As you have just spoken, and this is on page 6, line 17 of the transcript, saying that people from your area also went to Split for medical treatment, I wish to ask you whether you know whether other kinds of assistance arrived from Split, such as medicines, medical equipment, and so on of the same sort that you received from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did receive assistance from the clinical hospital in Split. I know this because during one of my visits to Mostar, and I can't say whether it was on the first or second visit, I found there a group of representatives of the Tuzla authorities who were just coming back from Split; and we had a conversation where they told me that we were receiving some assistance from there, and they also said that some of our wounded were being given medical treatment there. And this only goes to confirm what I said when answering the first question. This document is one I have not seen before, but I recognise the signature. I recognise Mr. Beslagic and Mr. Sead Avdic who were in the Logistics Centre. Whenever it was possible, everyone who gave us assistance was sent a letter of thanks, so I assume this was the case here too. This was sent to Dr. Dodig, the head of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for your response, and thank you for coming to testify here. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Petkovic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have completed the cross-examinations of the Defence teams of the other accused. Ms. West, would you prefer to have the break now and we start after the break, or would you like to start now?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I prefer to start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So do start. Ms. West, we have the binder, so you can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My name is Kim West. I'm an attorney with the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to ask you a few questions today. You indicated yesterday that you graduated from the Military Academy in 1971. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I graduated from the Military Academy in 1971. I completed the Command Staff Academy, a higher degree, in 1985, and after the war I was in the NATO school as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was your specialisation at the Academy.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After completing the Academy, my specialisation was communication and signals, and after graduating from the Command Staff Academy I was trained as a soldier, as a professional mass-murderer, I have to say, because all officers in the world, after completing this academy, are able to lead a huge war machinery which is used to kill if politics so decides. This means that I was appointed to the highest command duties, and to an even greater degree after my training in the NATO school.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But let's focus on communications. You said you specialised in communications at the academy, and in 1986, when you went to Tuzla, were you also a major in the Communications Department?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you move to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved to Tuzla after completing the Command Staff Academy, which was in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you first arrived in Tuzla, did you become a major in the Communications Department?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I became at first, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I live in Tuzla and Osijek, because we have a family farm near Osijek, where my wife was born. We spend about half of each month in Croatia, in Slavonia, and half of each month in Tuzla, where I have many obligations. I work in the management of Tuzla Airport. I'm the president of the Rotary Club and of several committees.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, sir, do you have children?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two children, a son who lives and works in Tuzla - he's married - and a daughter who lives and works in Canada, where she's married.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were they both born in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were born in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yesterday, you had indicated, in response to a question from Judge Antonetti -- he had asked you about the conflict in Central Bosnia, and in part of your answer, you said: "I worked for three years as a scientific adviser of the Institute for Investigating War Documents in Amsterdam, and in my work there I dealt with many of these issues." What years did you work in Amsterdam?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to clarify a little. I worked not as an adviser, but as a scientific associate under contract at the NIART [phoen], the Institute for Investigating War Documents in Amsterdam. The Parliament of the Kingdom of the Netherlands tasked this institute with a project which was investigating the role of DutchBat in Srebrenica and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I worked on this from 1999 until 2001 with a team of associates. In addition to this, I was also a scientific associate in the Institute for Investigating War Crimes for Dr. Smail Cekic in Sarajevo. I also had many duties, together with him, in throwing light on crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, thirdly, I had a contract working as a scientific associate of the Bosniak Institute in Sarajevo, with Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic for two years. I had a contract under which I was free, in my research, to choose my topic of research, and I was given office space in the institute to work in.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, as a result of this experience and this work that you did, did you have the opportunity to gain a broader perspective of what happened in the war? And what I mean by that is a perspective of what happened outside of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, in the course of my research I gained a very good picture of what had been happening in general and in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular segments in the course of the past war. When working for Dr. Smail Cekic in the Institute for Investigating War Crimes, which I mentioned, I gave papers in conferences organised by the institute; and one of my papers concerned the project of Greater Serbia, and the military methods used to implement that project. Another project I worked on was a seminar paper in my post-graduate studies, and it dealt with international -- the International Laws of War and the status of the protected zones -- protected areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When preparing this paper on the project of Greater Serbia, I made a thorough study of numerous documents, and I assert that all the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and before that in Croatia, did not occur by chance, but were the result of a project envisioned about 100 years ago. I drew attention to the need to study the writings of Serbian authors, starting with Garasanin onwards, and to link these up with the speeches made by Milosevic and Karadzic, and their actions, and what was done in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to ask you a bit about the demographics of the area from which you're -- where you live now in Tuzla. If we can look at P10068, it's a map, and if we can have map 39, please. It's going to come up on the screen in front of you. It might be the easiest way. So this is a map outlining the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sir, if you can go to actually in your book --

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I still don't seem to have the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you can actually look in your book. Why don't you go to 10068. You have it. There we go. So this is a map, an ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it also identifies areas outlined by the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. You can't see the bottom of the map, but I'll represent to you it says the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1991, and the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, 25 March 1993. Sir, I take it you're familiar with a general map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have to answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that is the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as a result of your experience in the war and also your studies and research afterwards, are you familiar generally with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I know of the plan, but I don't know the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine, we won't get into the details. But if you look at the map, you'll see that the areas 8 and 10, do you see those in front of you, those are generally the areas of Herceg-Bosna; and the area of 3, which is the Posavina, would you agree with me those were the areas that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan anticipated would go to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I knew about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and as soon as I saw it I didn't think it would survive, and this is what happened later on, and that's what I think now. I don't think it was a very clever plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, why didn't you think it was a clever plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, because of the people that devised it, and, secondly, because politics never envisaged Bosnia-Herzegovina that way, and it could never survive that way, as had been envisaged. But the only thing I recognise is that the -- is the policy and politics of Yalta, where Stalin and Churchill discussed world affairs, and when Churchill drew a line with his blue pen along the Drina and said, You're the East over there and you're the West. And the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was considered the West and could not be divided up as conceived by Vance-Owen or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is let's talk about the ethnicities of the municipalities as indicated by this map, and let's focus first on Tuzla, because that's where you spent the last 24 years. Would you agree with me that Tuzla is predominantly a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean when you say "Tuzla"? Do you mean the town of Tuzla itself, or the Tuzla canton, or the Tuzla region, because they are all different things and my answer will depend upon what you mean exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough. I mean the Tuzla municipality, so not the city of Tuzla but the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Tuzla municipality, the town of Tuzla proper, well, it's very difficult to deal with concepts that way. The town itself is mostly inhabited by Muslims. There's a Muslim majority, but all the local communes around there and if you look at the land registers, the land is owned mostly by Croats, so we would have to differentiate there in order to have the proper answer and would have to limit ourselves to the exact area we have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I gather it's your testimony that the town of Tuzla was predominantly Muslim, or the majority was Muslim, but the area around the area of Tuzla had a significant Croatian population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours and Madam Prosecutor, no, that's not right. When I say "the town," the town, I said, Yes, the Muslims were in the majority, the majority population in the town, but I said as for the land register, the Croatian population owned the land according to the land registers. I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to know who owned the land. I just generally want to know whether in the entire municipality of Tuzla, so we're not talking about only the town of Tuzla, but in the entire municipality of Tuzla, was there a Muslim relative majority?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look at the municipalities around Tuzla, and specifically I think the best way to do this is to talk about those municipalities that come under the 2nd Corps command. Yesterday, you mentioned a number of those, and let's go through those and others to see if they come under the 2nd Corps. Let's start in the lower -- well, let's start in Srebrenica. You can find that on the map; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I just thought about what you had just said, which is rather troublesome. On the map that we have, which was shown by Ms. West, as far as negotiations based in Geneva were concerned they were convinced that the entirety of the Tuzla area, as it is marked on the map, was predominantly Muslim. This is what appears on the key of the map. And you actually just said that in the town, indeed, Muslims were the majority population, but you added something regarding the land register. It may have gone off the wayside, but actually the land register reflects the various plots of land which belong to landowners, and I assume -- I've never been to Tuzla, but I assume that around the town of Tuzla you have fields where you have farmers working, because the Tuzla area is producing salt, I think that it's the number-one production item, but there must be some farmers producing vegetable and fruits; and if I understood correctly, according to you, the landowners of those agricultural plots were mainly Croats. Is that what you said to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Judge Antonetti, that's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It means that if those based in Geneva decide that the entirety of the Tuzla region, which is the area number 5 on the map, was going to be a Muslim area, of course it would lead to some problems for Croat landowners who seemed to have the entirety of the farming plots in the surrounding areas of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I understand what you said. Ms. West, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if we can just go back to those municipalities that were under the control of the 2nd Corps, and start with Srebrenica. Was that a municipality underneath or under the auspices of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that municipality was under the Tuzla district, and there was a municipal staff of the Territorial Defence there before the war and during the war. It was mostly physically separate, but it did come under the 2nd Corps. There was the 28th Division over there, and we know what the fate of that was with the events around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Srebrenica is a municipality with an absolute Muslim majority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, in Srebrenica at present there are 27 Croats living there. There's a Catholic Church. I was there quite recently, so I know this for certain. And you're quite right, the majority of the population was always the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We may need assistance from the usher, but I think that you can take the pen and mark on the screen, and as we go through these municipalities maybe you can just put a dot on each one that you agree falls under the 2nd Corps command. So if you can put a dot on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but do you want me to mark the municipalities that came under the 2nd Corps or do you mean the municipalities which came under the Tuzla district?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Municipalities that came under the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. [Marks] Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Bratunac has an absolute majority of Muslims in it as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you agree that Vlasenica has an absolute majority of Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So to go a little bit faster, let's do this in a group. Zvornik, Kalesija, Zivinice and Kladanj, those four in green above the red, are those all part of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't understand what you said. Zvornik -- I see it on the transcript. Zvornik, yes [Marks]. Kladanj [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just north of Kladanj, that municipality as well, do you see that? It's Z-i-v-i-n-i-c-e.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just to its east, the next municipality, Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are those municipalities also under the auspices of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't put it that way, exactly. The 2nd Corps was formed from the District Staff of the Territorial Defence. Before the war, all these municipalities, with their municipal staffs, came under the composition of the District Staff of Tuzla, and let me point out that that was before the war. Now, when the war broke out, after the decision by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to turn the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the armed force of Bosnia-Herzegovina, only 13 municipalities out of the pre-war ones that came under the district of Tuzla came under the command of the 2nd Corps, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a different question. Do you see all the municipalities in the area of number 5, going north-west towards Tuzla, so I'm not talking about Gorazde or Visegrad, not down there, but in the area right around Tuzla, all those municipalities in the number 5, are though all under the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can continue to explain, but I don't see why you don't want me to continue with these municipalities, Lukavac, Srebrenik, Gracanica, that was all 2nd Corps, Banovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Perfect. Then just on the map put a mark on each municipality that was part of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it in order. Srebrenik [Marks]. Then up there north of Tuzla, we have -- Your Honours, I said yesterday that under the 2nd Corps, for example, we had part of the Lopare municipality, and because part of it remained under Chetnik territory, so how do you want me to mark that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Maybe you can just put a "1" slash through it rather than an X. Just put a "1" through it.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, I'll put Lopare [Marks], the whole of Tuzla -- well, the whole of Lukavac, we can say that, yes [Marks], Banovici [Marks], Gracanica, part of the Gradacac municipality, so I'll put a 1 or half an X [Marks], part of the Brcko, the same thing, I'll put a 1 [Marks], part of the Doboj municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I have sort of a military question to ask you, because my attention is now drawn to the area where you have figure 6, which is a Serb area, Sekovici, can you see? Where you see the figure 6, can you confirm that this area was held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I would like us to draw a line here which was the boundary of the call line or the line towards the Serbs, and then this whole story would be clearer. For example, Sekovici municipality did not come under the call zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, since it's Ms. West who is examining you based on this map, I don't know whether this is of any use to you. Ms. West, the witness would like to draw a line which would be the front-line with the Serbs. Would that be of any use to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's -- I'm proposing this, because it's very difficult, looking at this map. This is the prewar situation. During the war, numerous municipalities were set up, and this map doesn't reflect that, doesn't correspond to that newly-arisen situation, so I'll try and do it. Although it's difficult technically, I'll try and do a separation line with the Chetniks so you can see what the 2nd Corps incorporated. Let's start with Gradacac municipality [Marks]. Perhaps I'm going to take a bigger portion here, but, anyway, Gracanica -- this is just a rough picture. Olovo [Marks] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could have a time-frame. What time is the gentleman speaking of? And when he refers to Chetniks, perhaps he can give us a clarification. Is this the VRS, and if so, I would appreciate that we don't use the pejorative term for Serbs as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yes. Yesterday, you made a clear distinction between the Chetniks and the Serbs, and earlier on you mentioned Chetniks. I conclude from this that, for you, those -- the people that occupied those front-lines were not the Serbs in the meaning you described yesterday, which were the JNA soldiers. So when you talk about Chetniks, what are you talking about, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "Chetnik," I'm mean something positive. At the beginning, the concept of Chetnik was something positive. Through history, let me put it this way, there were units -- there were units which fought for their freedom and their free territory, but in World War II and in this most recent war that we're discussing here and now, as far as we're concerned, the notion of Chetnik became something with a very negative connotation; and so I would like the Trial Chamber to understand that and respect that, because for me the term "Chetnik" does not mean a Serb. And let me say that my wife is a Serb, so if to no other reason, then for that reason; but also for the reason that I am a religious man myself and I respect each and every human being, regardless of their nation or creed or religion. So when I say "Chetnik" here, you can take that to mean the army. I don't know, was it the Republika Srpska Army, is that what it was called? Anyway, they were our enemies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, have you finished putting the front-line on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly, I'll draw it in. We have this part here [Marks], which was physically separated from us. I don't know if you can see that, but I've just drawn it in. It is the Tesanj and Maglaj and Zepce municipalities, where we had our BH Army brigades and also the 110th Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those municipalities are part -- are under the 2nd Corps as well; yes?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, not the municipalities, as such, but the military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if you can put an X on those areas as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes [Marks]. And then we have over here - I'll try and draw it in - part of the Srebrenica area [Marks]. It would be roughly this, if you can see it. So this largest part was a compact territory under the 2nd Corps, and we had two separate entities. Srebrenica was one and part of Tesanj and Maglaj formed the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. This is my question, a military type of question: You've just drawn the front-lines. My question is the following: How come that the area occupied by the Serbs, area number 6, why they are surrounded by you, because the is 2nd Corps is in the Srebrenica area and was also present north of that area held by the Serbs? Now, how come this Serb-held area managed to resist and did not fall under the command of the 2nd Corps, while you indicated yourself that you had 80.000 men in the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Your Honours, under the 2nd Corps composition, and I'll provide you with the precise information, at the beginning of the war we had 49.531 members. That was the first year of the war. In 1993, we had 77.647 soldiers. However, and I spoke about this yesterday, with that numerical supremacy, and we always had numerical supremacy in terms of soldiers and officers, we had 4.400 officers in the corps, the opposite side had absolute technical supremacy. And you know, and this is common knowledge, that after the withdrawal of the Yugoslav Army from Slovenia, most of those troops came to Bosnia. After Croatia, the same thing happened. Under the corps zone, specifically the one I've just depicted, and let me show you again the broader region around Zvornik and Sekovici, I'll draw a thicker line there [Marks], an armoured brigade from Jastrebarsko arrived. The armoured brigade from Jastrebarsko, according to its formation establishment, had over 100 tanks alone; and so, Your Honours, with great human suffering and all the rest of it, we managed to capture 27 tanks, I believe, and that was all the tanks we had. So in addition to the armoured brigade from Jastrebarsko and the broader region of South-East Bosnia, other armoured forces arrived. So as I said yesterday, to every one of our shells, they had a thousand of their own. One of our tanks, they had -- for one of our tanks, they had twenty-five. So the ratio was 1:25 there. So the line that we were able to establish, the defence line, we were able to hold throughout the war, and in 1993 and 1994 we managed to cross over into a tactical and operative offensive, and so we managed to expand the area of this territory. However, in 1992 and 1993, militarily speaking, it was absolutely impossible to do more than we managed to do, because the enemy forces were far greater. They had many more weapons, and you know that in 1992 the use of the air force came into play, and we didn't have an air force. So this was an unequal battle, looking at it on the basis of MTS, materiel and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've explained that the area covered by number 6 was -- you could not occupy it because there were 100 armoured vehicles there. Now, at the time, and this will be my last question, the solution could not be a military one, because you would never have managed to occupy these areas, so the solution could only be political; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. President, but could you repeat that question, please? I don't think I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'll repeat my question. You've just told us that in area number 6, there were 100 armoured vehicles. You managed to seize about 26, but about 80 were still remaining. And you've just told us that the Serbian forces were very numerous and very well equipped, which means that one could conclude, according to what you've told us, that the solution could not be a military one, you could not manage to beat the Serbs, and so the solution could only be a political one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your question is clear to me now, but let me make a correction. We did not capture 26 out of 100 tanks, but throughout the war, in other areas where we fought also, the total number of tanks we captured was 26. In addition to this, I have to add, to confirm what Your Honour said, and you can see this on the map, this side had unlimited assistance from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation][Previous translation continues] ... anything. I'm just asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if you are saying this, all the counsels will be up on their feet, so it's just a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, Your Honours, that a political solution was the only solution possible, and I felt that way before the war broke out. But unfortunately it did not materialise, so we did whatever we were able to, as soldiers. What politicians were able to do, I cannot comment on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're asking about number 6, but there are three areas marked "6," and at least in the interpretation into Croatian, it seems that you consider the Serbs had a sort of enclave in number 6, but this was all held by them, and it was actually the 2nd Corps that was encircled. So they had tactical manoeuvres in all the areas marked "6."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, General Praljak is right, there are three number 6s here, but my question is regarding area number 6 in the middle. Well, I can't really see now. The one really in the middle, just -- the Kovaci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understood you, and that's the area I was thinking of also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had the same area in mind. Very good, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, actually, there are four number 6s on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, there are four, but we were talking about the "6" really at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to the map, and let's finish up what I originally asked you, which is: Put an X in the municipalities that were under the auspices of the 2nd Corps. So I think probably the last place that we're talking about is the Posavina area. Is that part -- was that part of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, a part of Posavina did belong to the 2nd Corps to the south of Brcko. I'm drawing a line here [Marks], and this is where we kept trying to break through the enemy corridor and reach the Sava River, and then the area you referred to as Posavina would have belonged to us. But the actual area of the corps was as I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So would you agree with me of the areas you have marked, they mostly appear to be green; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in regard to the blue areas, at least in the Posavina, we do have some blue municipalities in the very north -- northern Posavina. Is it your testimony that those are Croatian areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how Madam Prosecutor -- I don't know what she means when she said "Croatian." It's all Bosnia-Herzegovina. But if you're asking about the colour, yes, those areas are blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I will be more precise in my question. Are those municipalities -- was that the ethnic make-up of those municipalities, was it a majority of Croats living there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't be certain about that, but I think that's correct. And if that's how it's represented on the map, I assume that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right, sir. If we can -- we're going to take a break shortly, but I think we can finish this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to have an IC number for this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked version of the map shall be given Exhibit IC00964. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, let's continue to look at this map, and if you can look down to the areas that are number 8 and number 10. Would you agree with me that that area on the map is what was considered Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, but I object because the Croatian Community of Soli, Posavina, Sarajevo, and Central Bosnia also belonged to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as of the 17th of October, 1992; so I think the question is not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine. Madam Nozica, you should not here testify. Let Ms. West proceed, and then if you have questions at the end, you can put additional questions. So, Ms. West, please put your question again, because we've lost track.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that that question [sic] be stricken from the record as testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the purposes of this question, if we can look to the areas of 8 and 10. Do you see those areas in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see areas 8 and 10 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let's assume, for the purposes of my question, that municipalities covered in blue -- coloured in blue are those that have an absolute majority of Croats in them. Do you see several blue municipalities in the area of 8 and 10?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the areas marked blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that most of those areas are actually buttressed or at least sided to the west with Croatia; they are close up to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the rest of 8 and 10, would you agree that there is not so much blue; a lot of 8 and 10 in the middle area would be, for the purposes of this question, the green-coloured areas as Muslim areas? The question is: Those areas are mostly green; correct? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to object to this line of questioning. I think that the Prosecutor is asking the witness to speculate and to interpret the colours on the map. The witness said that he had no personal knowledge of where there was a majority and where a minority population -- we can all see what the colours are on the map. All the witness is saying is, I have to trust the map. The witness was not told who compiled this map for what purpose, and the witness cannot know whether he can or cannot trust the map if he has no personal knowledge of the make-up of the population in areas other than the area he lived and worked in. That's why I'm objecting to this line of questioning, and I don't see what it's leading up to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the reason that in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's the reason in the question I said "for the purposes of this question." I would not ask this witness, who's lived in Tuzla for the last 24 years, if he has an intimate knowledge of the majority ethnic groups in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do support my learned friend -- my learned friend's interjection at the outset. The map really does speak for itself. Nothing more needs to be said, and if my learned friend for the Prosecution wishes to ask precise questions, of course there is no objection; but asking a very subjective evaluation, for example, in the area delineated in number 8, subjectively is it more blue or more green, it really doesn't take us very far. The map shows what it shows, and I would ask my learned friend to move on and ask precise questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, the map seemingly was drawn on the basis of the census of 1991, so those people that plotted the map had those figures from the census of 1991, from 1 to 10, as part of the Vance-Owen Plan. They marked this map with a colour code which matched the ethnic composition at the time, so what we see here cannot be challenged, since it is based on the census of 1991. If you put the question to him and say, In Livno, there was 50 percent Croats, he can only say, Yes. What is more interesting, however, is the question you want to put to him; so please go to the point and put your question. My colleague says it would be best after the break, so let's have the break, so you can prepare your question, and we shall meet again in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the map is still in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look you up, you would agree with me to the right of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although it's not in red, this is Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that the area in number 4 that is red, that's an area that the Serbian controlled; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it is on the map. That's how it's represented on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In 1992, is it your memory that the Serbs controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would object. We should be careful here. This is a map, as you rightly said so, Your Honour, based on a census of population, and Vance-Owen Plan is projected on that, so this is not the reality. This is simply a plan, and the witness might be very easily confused by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please break down your questions and ask the witness whether, according to what he knows, area number 4 in 1992 and 1993 was controlled by the Serbs or not, because we know that in area 4 there was a majority of Serbs. Whether this area was controlled by the Serb Army, I don't know, but maybe he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the area on the map that's number 2, and the number 2 is right in the middle of Banja Luka, in 1992 was this an area that was predominantly controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you mean in military terms, under the control of the Serbs? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard of the Posavina corridor before; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of the Posavina corridor. I don't know what you mean by it. The Posavinski corridor, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the area between, for the purposes of the question, number 4 and number 2, which is a thin piece of land that is not -- mostly in red, and it's number 3, would you consider that to be the Posavina? You have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area marked with the number 3 on the map which I see before me is one part of Posavina, only one part of it. Posavina is a much broader concept.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough. But in 1992, you were in the 2nd Corps and you were fighting in this particular area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in what area, in Posavina or in the area we marked a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Witness. I'll be very specific. Let's talk about the area of Brcko. Do you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in 1992, was there fighting in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the time Arkan and his units entered Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in 1992, was there also fighting in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 there was also fighting in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, if you can tell us, what was the fighting about? Or, rather, strike that. Who were the parties involved in the fight?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, it could hardly be called "combat." It was a slaughter of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Witness, let's just back up for a second. So my first question is: Who were the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens and the paramilitary Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were the citizens --

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, a correction. When I say "citizens," I'm referring to unarmed civilians, because it was not actually a fight, it was not combat. The civilians were simply killed in the streets of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at P10894, and you can open it up in your binder. P10894. We can read this -- the beginning of this together, and I'm going to ask you some questions as we go along. This is a May 9th, 1993, AP article, and it begins that: "The pipeline from Serbia that has kept Bosnian Serb rebels well supplied spits out its last few drops here in Serb-controlled south-western Croatia. "Those drops mean life to Knin, capital of the Serbs' self-proclaimed Krajina republic in Croatia, and the birthplace of the uprising three years ago that preceded savage [indiscernible] war in Croatia and Bosnia. "To cut supplies to the Bosnian Serbs, as Yugoslavia has vowed to do, would weaken this furthest outpost of Serb-held territory in former Yugoslavia as well. It would be more vulnerable to Croatian government forces that are determined to regain control of the land ..." Let's just stop there. Here it's talking about a pipeline and about an area where there was an effort to cut supplies. Would you agree with me that that pipeline is in the area of the Posavina that we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from this document I see that mention is made of South-Western Croatia. It's not about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, let's go back. Let's go back to the question that I asked, and I'll read it to you again. Would you agree with me that the pipeline is in the area of the Posavina and that's what we just talked about? So the question is focusing on pipeline.

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, please excuse me, but for me a pipeline is for oil. What is this about? I don't understand this at all, and I see that this is about Croatia, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we'll read a little bit more, and then maybe you can determine what this is about. It goes on to say: "'We call it the corridor of life,' said Vice-Premier Bronco Ljubovic of the Croatia-Serb self-proclaimed government. He and other Serb leaders spoke to the reporter during a visit Thursday and Friday. Serb-domination Yugoslavia announced on Thursday under intense international pressure that it would cut off supplies to the Bosnian Serbs after they once again refused to endorse an international peace plan. One of the Bosnian Serbs' main objections to the plan is that it would force them to turn over to the United Nations a narrow corridor across Northern Bosnia that supplied Serb-controlled areas centred around Banja Luka." Mr. Makar, my question to you is: This narrow corridor to which this article refers, is this the corridor that goes across the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can only agree that that was what the Serbs called it, that's how they referred to it in their news broadcasts. We did not refer to it by that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How did you refer to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't refer to it at all. We fought there on a territory, and for a long time in the beginning there was no corridor there for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Makar. I'm sure this is just a misunderstanding between the two of us, but you said that, We did not refer to it by that name. And then I said, How did you refer to it? And then you said: "We didn't refer to it at all. We fought there on a territory, and for a long time from the beginning there was no corridor there for the Serbs." Sir, my question is only: Do you recognise that there was a corridor in the Posavina area that provided military supplies and other supplies to the Serbs in the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's open to discussion, and it's very hard to provide a response to that. We held that territory under artillery fire throughout the time, so that any passage there would have been highly risky and there would have been huge casualties, because the 2nd Corps, since it had insufficient MTS, artillery and tanks, had very strong artillery support from the forces of Operative Group Bosnian Posavina, Orasje. They had strong artillery forces, so one could hardly speak of a corridor. It was more like a death road for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, on this death road, was there heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So you have personal knowledge of the fighting going on over this death road?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do, and unfortunately very bad memories, because dozens of people were killed right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. How long were you posted there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps was always where there was the most fierce fighting, and wherever there was such fighting, forward command posts were established. Just to clarify to Their Honours and Madam Prosecutor, that would be a group of officers with certain communications equipment which would go to that part of the zone of the 2nd Corps where there was the heaviest fighting in order to be able to get an overview of the situation directly, establish direct communication with the front-line. And I was posted there at the head of one such group of officers throughout the second half of 1992, almost throughout that entire period, and in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And even after you left that post, the fighting continued; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting never stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue with this article. It says: "The 220-mile-long --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly read slowly for the sake of the interpreters and the court reporter, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, apologies. "The 220-mile-long corridor runs from Knin, Croatia, across the top of Bosnia to Serbia proper in the east. It is narrowest south of Brcko and northern Bosnia near the Serbian Croatian border; and that area has seen heavy fighting throughout the war. The patchwork of territory seized in a year of gives the Serbs no other way to keep arms, fuel, food and other goods flowing through much of Bosnia." Mr. Makar, would you agree with me that the Serbs used this death road, as you called it, to supply Serbian-held areas in Western Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, I don't know what the Serbs did and whether they supplied those areas that you're referring to. What was important, as far as I was concerned, that anybody trying to pass through that territory, that we targeted them if they attempted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Croatia would have a concern if the Serbs were using a corridor for supplies and fuel and food?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't really answer that. I can just give you my opinion, and I don't think my opinion is important, what Croatia thought. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Makar, you told us about the research you've done about the war and you've also agreed that you have a general perspective of what went on in the war, and you left the BiH as a brigadier general. So are you telling this Trial Chamber that you have no knowledge of what the other parties designed or had goals for in the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not true that I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's try again. Would you agree with me that Croatia would have a concern if the Serbs were using the corridor for supplies and fuel and food?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't wish to be testifying or anything, but perhaps the question, if it was phrased a little bit tighter. It's overly broad, concerned for what reason. And perhaps she could lay the factual predicate so the gentleman could then understand exactly what she's asking the gentleman to opine on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the gentleman was about to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, try and be as accurate as you can. I must humbly say that I don't understand what you are getting at. I don't understand what the purpose of all this is. Maybe things will become clearer over the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Makar, go ahead. I had asked you: "Would you agree with me that the Croatians would have had a concern if the Serbs had used the corridor for supplies and fuel and food?" And you started to answer. What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: ANDJELKO MAKAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tried to answer the Prosecutor, Madam West, in the first hour of this discussion. Now, the Prosecutor interrupted me. If she wishes me to give my own analysis of this matter, then that would need special preparation on my part. Now, individual questions as to what this would mean for Croatia, what wouldn't it mean, I don't think I'd like to speculate on an individual basis like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise to my learned friend Madam West, but as a question hasn't been asked, I'd like to raise a general objection. We have a witness about the facts, he's here to testify about the facts, and I think that the questions that the Prosecutor is asking him now, as to what he learnt later on and what he investigated later on, are questions which can be asked of an expert witness, but about a fact -- but when we have a fact witness, I don't think that is in order, to ask a witness about subsequent knowledge. And then we are delving in politics. And asked several times by the Judges as well, he said that he can only speak about military matters, so I think -- and I'd like to add that -- and I didn't get up to my feet to object, because I know that the Prosecutor has ample leeway in trying to discredit the witness, but we didn't even approach any of these questions during the examination-in-chief. So I would like to object and say that these questions go far, far beyond the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I have quite a lot of experience in criminal cases over the last few years. I put these questions to him to see whether he could provide us with any additional information on questions of a strategic or political nature. Every time, he answered by saying that he was a military man, could only answer very accurate questions. This is what he answered. With the knowledge you have, you try and get back to this and address his profession, and you're wasting your time, because he says, I don't know. Defence counsel then get to their feet and raise objections, so we're wasting our time. It would be better for you to get straight to the point. That would be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has indicated to us that he was a soldier in the field, and in fact he was in the exact area I'm talking about and he saw people die. And he says that the only reason he was there were to kill the Serbs going by. I find it unusual that this gentleman, who not only has given us military information, who has given us plenty of political information with regard to the Croatian Community of Soli, and someone who has done research on war --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't say the Serbs, I never said "Serbs." I apologise for having to intervene there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. My point is, Your Honour, I find it difficult for this gentleman to indicate to us that he only had an understanding of the people that he was trying to kill in front of them, whether they be Serbs or not, and not what the importance of this actual corridor was for. It's highly unusual that a person of this intelligence, of this experience, wouldn't know what is going on behind the fighting, so it seems quite unusual. And I'll also say the objection that this goes beyond the scope of the direct seems also to be an unusual objection, certainly in the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours. This entire exchange began with the question concerning Croatia, and I assume she means the Republic of Croatia, and of course which had its own share of problems at the time in and around that area. I put precisely my objection that she needs to be more specific, exactly what she's trying to get at, and when she's talking about Serbs, she's talking about Croatia, she's talking about this corridor, what is she trying to get at, number 1. Number 2, why is it relevant to the Prosecution's case, which is probably more important, because yesterday we got a lecture from Mr. Scott, who is behind her, telling us that the Defence is wasting their time, and now it appears that we are either in a fishing expedition or we're dealing with historical matters that have nothing to do with the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
